A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a cyberattack intended to make a machine or network resource unavailable by overwhelming it with superfluous requests, thereby preventing legitimate use. A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack amplifies this threat by coordinating an influx of traffic from many different sources, making mitigation more complex. The history of these attacks dates to 1996 with a SYN flood against Panix and has since evolved to include massive, record-breaking incidents targeting major corporations, cloud providers, and cultural platforms like the Internet Archive. Attack motivations range from criminal profit and state-sponsored aggression to hacktivism and revenge. The continuous escalation in scale, evidenced by attacks measured in terabits per second and hundreds of millions of requests per second, demonstrates the persistent and growing challenge these attacks pose to global network security.
